                Notary Public: Batangas Province

text:
MANUAL OF SPECIFICATIONS - LIPA BARAKO COFFEE

                1. Geographical Area
                The coffee must be grown exclusively in Lipa City, Batangas
                within the specified coordinates and altitude ranges.

                2. Soil Requirements
                Volcanic soil with pH 6.0-6.5, rich in organic matter
                Well-drained terrain, moderate slope

                3. Climate Conditions
                Temperature range: 18-24°C
                Rainfall: 2000-2500mm annually
                Distinct dry season for proper harvesting

                4. Cultivation Standards
                Traditional farming practices preserved
                No chemical pesticides during flowering
                Harvest period: October to January

                5. Quality Standards
                Moisture content: 11-12%
                Bean size: 17-19 screen
                Cup quality: Distinct Barako flavor profile

                Certified by: Bureau of Plant Industry
                Notarized: Republic of the Philippines

text:
Lesson 8
The Global Media Cultures 
Globalization and identity, globalization and human rights, globalization and culture, or globalization and terrorism are some concepts related to the study of globalization by many scholars. 

Situations created through globalization and media make people conceive they belong to one world called Global Village, a term coined by Marshall MacLuhan in early 1960’s, a Canadian media theorist, to express the idea that people throughout the world are interconnected through the use of new media technologies. 
According to scholars, the world is globalized in the 1900s upon the advancement of media and transportation technology. 

Globalization and Media - Globalization which refers to economic and political integration on a world scale, has a crucial cultural dimension in which the media has the central role. 
Five Time Periods in the Study of Globalization and Media
1. Oral Communication - Globalization as a social process is characterized by the existence of global economic, political, cultural, linguistic and environmental interconnections and flows that make the many of the currently existing borders and boundaries irrelevant.
	Human speech is the oldest and most enduring.
Languages as a means to develop the ability to communicate across culture are the lifeline of globalization
Without language there would be no globalization; without globalization there would be no world languages
2. Script Writing - is humankind’s principal technology for collecting, manipulating, storing, retrieving, communicating and disseminating information. Writing may have been invented independently three times in different parts of the world: in the Near East, China and Mesoamerica.
Cuneiform script - created in Mesopotamia, present-day Iraq, is the only writing system which can be traced to its earliest prehistoric origin.
clay tokens - This antecedent of the cuneiform script was a system of counting and recording goods with it. 
script- the very first writing. Humans communicate and shared knowledge and ideas through it.
The origin of writing was in the form of carvings such as wood, stone, bones and others. 
Script of Ancient Egyptian written in papyrus (plant). 
3. The Printing Press -The printing press is a device that allows for the mass production of uniform printed matter, mainly text in the form of books, pamphlets and newspapers. It revolutionized society in China where it was created.
Johannes Gutenberg further developed this in the 15th century with his invention of the Gutenberg press.
4. Electronic Media - It refers to the broadcast or storage media that take advantage of electronic technology. They may include television, radio, internet, fax, CD-ROMs, DVD, and any other medium that requires electricity or digital encoding of information. The term electronic media is often used in contrast with print media.
5. Digital Media - Phones and television are now considered digital while computer is considered the most important media influencing globalization. Computers give access to global and market place and transformed cultural life. The following are the companies involved in globalization: Microsoft, Apple, Google, and Facebook.

Popular Music and Globalization
Music - participates in the reinforcing of boundaries of culture and identity.
Popular music - explains the complex dynamics of globalization not only because it is popular but music is highly mediated, is deeply invested in meaning and has proven to be an extremely mobile and resourceful capital
World music - is defined as the umbrella category which various types of traditional and non Western music are produced for Western consumption.

Lesson 9
The Globalization of Religion 
Globalization implicates religions in several ways. It calls forth religious response and interpretation. Religions played important roles in bringing about and characterizing globalization. Among the consequences of this implication for religion is that globalization encourages religious pluralism.

Religions - identify themselves in relation to one another, and they become less rooted in particular places because of diasporas and transnational ties.

Perspectives on the Role of Religion in the Globalization Process
1. The Modernist Perspective. It is the perspective of most intellectuals and academics. Its view is that all secularizations would eventually look alike and the different religions would all end up as the same secular and “rational” philosophy. It sees religion revivals as sometimes being a reaction to the Enlightenment and modernization.
2. Post-Modernist Perspective. It rejects the Enlightenment, modernist values of rationalism, empiricism, and science, along with the Enlightenment, modernist structures of capitalism, bureaucracy, and even liberalism. The core value of post-modernism is expressive individualism. The post-modernist perspective can include “spiritual experiences,” but only those without religious constraints.
3. The Pre-Modernist Perspective. - It is best represented and articulated by the Roman Catholic Church, especially by Pope John Paul II. The Pope’s understanding is drawn from his experiences with Poland, but it encompasses events in other countries as well. Each religion has secularized in its own distinctive way, which has resulted in its own distinctive secular outcome. This suggests that even if globalization brings about more secularization, it will not soon bring about one common, global worldview.
Secularization is understood as a shift in the overall frameworks of human condition; it makes it possible for people to have a choice between belief and non belief in a manner hitherto unknown

Transnational Religion and Multiple Glocalization
Transnational religion is a means of describing solutions to new-found situations that people face as a result of migration and it comes as two quite distinct blends of religious universalism and local particularism.
Transnational National Communities are constructed and religious hierarchies perform dual religious and secular functions that ensure the groups’ survival
Fundamentalist or revivalist movement - attempt to construct pure religion that sheds the cultural tradition in which past religious life was immersed
Indigenization, hybridization or glocalization are processes that register the ability of religion to mould into the fabric of different communities in ways that connect it intimately with communal and local relations
Global -local or glocal religion represents a genre of expression, communication and individual identities. It involves the consideration of an entire range of responses as outcomes instead of a single master narrative of secularization and modernization
Forms of Glocalization
1. Indigenization is connected with the specific faiths with ethnic groups whereby religion and culture were often fused into a single unit. It is also connected to the survival of particular ethnic groups.
2. Vernacularization involved the rise of vernacular language endowed with the symbolic ability of offering privileged access to the sacred and often promoted by empires.
3. Nationalization connected the consolidation of specific nations with particular confessions and has been a popular strategy both in Western and eastern Europe.
4. Transnationalization complemented religious nationalization by forcing groups to identify with specific religious traditions of real or imagine national homelands or to adopt a more universalist vision of religion.

Lesson 10
Global City: Its Definition and Concepts
global city is an urban centre that enjoys significant competitive advantages and that serves as a hub within a globalized economic system. The term has its origins in research on cities carried out during the 1980s, which examined the common characteristics of the world’s most important cities.

What constitutes a global city were primarily economic. As such, New York, London, and Tokyo can be identified as global cities, all of which are hubs of global finance and capitalism.

Indicators of a Global City
1. Seats of Economic Power - Cities that have a strong influence on global finance, business, and trade may be considered seats of economic power.
New York may have the largest stock market in the world but 
Tokyo houses the most number of corporate headquarters (613 company headquarters as against 217 in New York, its competitor). 
Shanghai plays a critical role in the global economic supply chain ever since China has become the manufacturing center of the world. Shanghai has the world’s busiest container port, moving over 33 million container units in 2013.
2. Centers of Authority - Cities where important government decisions are made may be considered centers of authority.
Washington DC it is the seat of American state power. People around the world know its major landmarks: the White House, the Capitol Building (Congress), the Supreme Court, the Lincoln Memorial, and the Washington Monument. 
Canberra is a sleepy town and thus is not as attractive to tourists. But as Australia’s political capital, it is home to the country’s top politicians, bureaucrats, and policy advisors.
3. Centers of Political Influence - Cities that house major international organizations may also be considered centers of political influence. 
The headquaters of the United Nations is in New York, and that of the European Union is in Brussels. An influential political city near the Philippines is Jakarta, also the location of the main headquarters of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). 
Powerful political hubs exert influence on their own countires as well as on international affairs. European Central Bank which oversees the Euro (the European Union’s currency), is based in Frankfurt.
4. Centers of Higher Learning and Culture - A city’s intellectual influence is seen through the influence of its publishing industry. 
Many of the books that people read are published in places like New York , London, or Paris. 
The New York Times carries the name of New York City but it is far from being a local newspaper. 
One of the reasons for many tourists visiting Boston is that they want to see Harvard University - the world’s top university. 
Los Angeles, the center of the American film industry may also be considered a global city. Copenhagen is considered as one of the culinary capitals of the world, with its top restaurants incommensurate with its size. 
Manchester, England in the 1980’s was a dreary, industrial city. But many prominent post-punk and New Wave bands - Joy Division, the Smiths, the Happy Mondays - hailed from this city, making it a global household name. In Southeast Asia, Singapore is slowly becoming a cultural hub for the region. It now houses some of the region’s top television stations and news organization (MTV Southeast Asia and Channel News Asia). Its various art galleries and cinemas also show paintings from artists and filmmakers respectively from the Philippines and Thailand. It is, in fact, sometimes easier to watch the movie of a Filipino indie filmmaker in Singapore than it is in Manila.

Cities as Engines of Globalization 
Cities - are the engines of globalization. They are social magnets, growing faster and faster. 
Global Cities - An increasing number of large cities, with populations of over five million, cities that are nodes of global as much as national networks. 
In 2000, there were 18 megacities (over 10 million) ‚ such as Mumbai, Tokyo, New York City/Newark 
Mexico City had populations in excess of 10 million inhabitants. 
Greater Tokyo already has 35 million. 
The Hong Kong/Guangzhow area is even larger, perhaps 120 million.

Lesson 11
Global Demography: Meaning and Its Origin
DEMOGRAPHY refers to the study of populations, with reference to size and density, fertility, mortality, growth, age distribution, migration, and vital statistics and the interaction of all these with social and economic conditions. (Cited by Tulchinsky)

Demography was derived from the Greek words demos for “population” and graphia for “description” or “writing,” thus the phrase, “writings about population.” It was coined by Achille Guillard, a Belgian statistician, in 1855. However, the origins of modern demography can be traced back to the John Graunt’s analysis of ‘Bills of Mortality’ which was published in 1662.

Demographic transition 
• started in mid- or late 1700’s in Europe.
• High birth & death rates → Low birth & death rates
• death rates and fertility began to decline	

• High to low Fertility - 200 years in France and 100 years in the United States.
• Asia & Africa
Began later (20th century)
Mortality decline: Happened in Africa & Asia (except Japan earlier)
India - Life expectancy: ~24 years (early 1900s)
China - Same life expectancy level (1929–1931) 
Fertility decline: 
Japan - Fertility remained high until 1930s
Rapid population growth after World War II

Effect of Demographic Transition
A remarkable effect of the demographic transition is ‘the enormous gap in life expectancy that emerged between Japan and the West on the one hand and the rest of the world on the other.
1820 - the life expectancy at birth of Japan and the West was 12 years greater than that of other countries. 1900 - It increased by 20 years
1900-1950 - Improvement in life expectancy all throughout the world, the gap had reached 22 years.
1999 - the gap declined to 14 years. 

19th century: 
Europe and the West - had an increased in share in the world’s population, from 22.0 percent to 33.0 percent.
Asia and Oceania - contribution dropped from 69.0 percent to 56.7.
India and China suffered from economic stagnation and decline during that time.

20th century as Africa, Asia, Latin America, and Oceania had high levels of population growth rates.
Between 1820 and 1980 - 69.3 percent of the world’s population growth occurred in Europe and Western
Between 1950 and 2000 - only 11.7 percent occurred in the region.
The United States projected that population growth will be shifted toward Africa. It is estimated that by 2150
In 2150 there will be a projected increase of two billion if we combine the population of Asia, Latin America, and Oceania.
Age Structure, the overall trend in Japan and the West was downward until 1950. Their dependency ratio was close to 0.5. It only increased

Developing Countries like India and the Philippines had higher dependency ratios than the West in 1900.
Dependency ratios started to disappear because there is a decline in global birth rate.

Theory of Demographic Transition
Demographic transition theory suggests that future population growth will develop along a predictable four- or five-stage model.
1.Stage 1, pre-industrial society, death rates and birth rates are high and roughly in balance.
Example: United States in the 1800s. All human populations are believed to have had this balance until the late 18th century, when this balance ended in Western Europe. 
Growth rates were less than 0.05% since Agricultural Revolution over 10,000 years ago
Population growth is typically very slow in this stage, because the society is constrained by the available food supply; therefore, unless the society develops new technologies to increase food production (e.g. discovers new sources of food or achieves higher crop yields), any fluctuations in birth rates are soon matched by death rates.
2.Stage 2, Developing Stage that of a developing country, death rates drop rapidly due to improvements in food supply and sanitation, which increase life spans and reduce disease. Afghanistan is currently in this stage.
The improvement in this stage includes selective breeding, crop rotation, farming techniques, access to technology, basic healthcare, and education.
In Europe, the death rate decline started in the late 18th century in northwestern Europe and spread to the south and east over approximately the next 100 years. Without a corresponding fall in birth rates this produces an imbalance, and the countries in this stage experience a large increase in population.
3.Stage 3 Birth rates Fall. Birth rates decrease due to various fertility factors such as access to contraception, increases in wages, urbanization, a reduction in subsistence agriculture, an increase in the status and education of women, a reduction in the value of children’s work, an increase in parental investment in the education of children and other social changes. Mexico’s population is at this stage
The birth rate decline in developed countries started in the late 19th century in northern Europe.
4. Stage 4 Industrial Stage, there are both low birth rates and low death rates. 
Birth rates may drop to well below replacement level as has happened in countries like Germany, Italy, and Japan, leading to a shrinking population, a threat to many industries that rely on population growth.
Death rates may remain consistently low or increase slightly due to increases in lifestyle diseases due to low exercise levels and high obesity and an aging population in developed countries.
By the late 20th century, birth rates and death rates in developed countries leveled off at lower rates
5. Stage 5 (Debated). Some scholars delineate a separate fifth stage of below-replacement fertility levels. Others hypothesize a different stage five involving an increase in fertility.
United Nations Population Fund (2008) categorizes nations as high-fertility, intermediate-fertility, or low-fertility.
The United Nations (UN) anticipates the population growth will triple between 2011 and 2100 in high-fertility countries, which are currently concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa.
For countries with intermediate fertility rates (the United States, India, and Mexico all fall into this category), growth is expected to be about 26 percent.
Low-fertility countries like China, Australia, and most of Europe will actually see population decline of approximately 20 percent.

ACTIVITY: Comparison  
Explain and give simple examples: 
Symmetric vs. Asymmetric vs. Hashing vs. Signatures 
1. Symmetric Encryption 
➢ Symmetric encryption is a type of cryptography where only one key is used 
to both encrypt and decrypt data.  
➢ Both sender and the receiver must share the same secret key before they 
can communicate securely. 
➢ This method is fast and efficient, but it can be risky if the shared key is 
exposed. 
• Example: 
o You save a document on your laptop and protect it with a 
password. When you lock the file, the system uses that 
password to encrypt the document. When you want to open it 
again, you enter the same password to decrypt it. Anyone who 
knows the password can also access the file. 
2. Asymmetric Encryption 

REPUBLIC OF THE PHILIPPINES 
Polytechnic University of the Philippines 
OFFICE OF THE VICE PRESIDENT FOR CAMPUSES 
Sto. Tomas Campus 
 
➢ 
Asymmetric encryption is a type of cryptography that uses two 
different keys: a public key and a private key. 
➢ The public key is used to encrypt data, while the private key is used to 
decrypt it. 
➢ This makes communication more secure because only the owner of the 
private key can access the message 
• Example: 
o when you enter your credit card details on a shopping website, 
your browser uses the website’s public key to encrypt the 
information before sending it. Only the website’s server, which 
has the private key, can decrypt and read your payment details 
securely. 
3. Hashing 
➢ Hashing is a process that converts data into a fixed-length value called a 
hash. 
➢ It is a one-way process, meaning the original data cannot be retrieved from 
the hash. 
➢ Even a small change in the input will produce a completely different hash 
value. 
• Example: 
o When you register your fingerprint, the system converts it into a 
hash value and stores it. When you try to unlock your phone, 
your fingerprint is scanned again and hashed, then compared 
to the stored hash to check if it matches. 
4. Digital Signatures 
➢ Digital signatures are used to verify the identity of the sender and ensure 
data integrity. 
➢  It uses asymmetric encryption, where the sender signs using a private key 
and the receiver verifies using a public key. 
➢ This ensures that the message is authentic and has not been altered. 
• Example: 
o when a company sends you an official email, it includes a 
digital signature created using its private key. Your email 
system can use the company’s public key to verify that the 
message really came from them and was not changed during 
transmission.

Optimizing QR code readability for curved agro-food packages using response surface methodology to improve mobile phone-based traceability
Jianping Qian , Bin Xing , Baohui Zhang , Han Yang 


Introduction
Several paradigm-shifting events, including the bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) case in the early to mid-1990s (Wales, Harvey, & Warde, 2006) and the dioxin contamination of chicken feed in Belgium in 1999 (Bernard et al., 2002), have drawn attention on food safety over the past decades (Bertolini, Bevilacqua, & Massini, 2006). At the same time, consumer demand for fresh-like, safe, and nutritious food is increasing (Ramesh, Nayak, Amirbahman, Tripp, & Mukhopadhyay, 2016). The ISO 22005:2007 food traceability standard requires each company to identify both its suppliers and customers, a concept based on the principle of one-up, one-down (International Organization for Standardization, 2007). Driven by food safety, quality, regulatory, social, economic, and technological concerns, voluntary and mandatory traceability systems are now being enforced worldwide (Boys & Fraser, 2018; Jin & Zhou, 2014; Kim & Woo, 2016).
Traceable unit identification is very important for achieving traceability. Identification technologies, including barcodes and radio frequency identification (RFID), can be integrated into a supply chain system as traceable unit identification methods (Fan et al., 2019; Jedermann, Praeger, & Lang, 2017; Ruiz-Garcia & Lunadei, 2011). Because of their low cost and ease of use, barcodes have become widely used in retail over the last 30 years and now facilitate inventory control, stock recording, and checkout (Ghaani, Cozzolino, Castelli, & Farris, 2016). A barcode is a one-dimensional pattern of parallel spaces and bars arranged to represent 10 digits. The information encoded in the barcode can be read by an optical barcode scanner that sends the information to a system where it is stored and processed. Two-dimensional (2D) barcodes store more information than one-dimensional barcodes because they consist of a combination of dots and spaces arranged in a 2D array or matrix in lieu of bars and spaces (Qian et al., 2012).
Quick response (QR) codes are typical 2D barcodes and are defined by the industrial ISO/IEC 18004:2006 standard (Jiao, Zou, & Li, 2017). Recently, some tamper-proof barcode indicators that provide time and temperature information have been designed (Schumann & Schmid, 2018). Each QR code is composed of dark (logical “1″) and light (logical “0″) modules that are evenly distributed over a square net of fields, wherein the size of a field is the size of a single module. According to the ISO/IEC 18,004 standard (International Organization for Standardization, 2006), the size of one module is 4 × 4 pixels with a print resolution of 300 dots per inch. This size ensures readability by most optical devices.
In addition, the information collected and searched using portable devices, including mobile phones, has become an effective means for improving management effects (So-In, Poolsanguan, & Rujirakul, 2014; Tseng et al., 2006). Steinberger, Rothmund, and Auernhammer (2009) developed mobile farming information collection equipment that transmitted information to the server via the internet. Li, Qian, Yang, Sun, and Ji (2010) developed for cucumber traceability a farming information-acquisition technique and a record-keeping and decision-support system based on a personal digital assistant, which was produced in two production companies in Beijing and helped improved production efficiency. Qian, Xing, Wu, Chen, and Wang (2018) incorporated image processing technology in a smartphone to develop a simple, inexpensive, and rapidly accessible system to estimate apple yield.
Recently, scanning QR codes attached to agro-food using mobile phones has become a convenient traceability method. Improving QR code readability for different conditions is important for information acquisition and to ensure a satisfactory customer experience. Tarjan, Senk, Tegeltija, Stankovski, and Ostojic (2014) used an Android smartphone to analyze the readability of QR codes with variable content, sizes, and data error correction levels. The results show that the readability of the QR code is not directly affected by the number of coded characters or by the error correction level. However, the readability of the QR code is affected by the size of the modules comprising the code.
Existing studies and applications provide solid evidence for using QR code labels attached to regular surfaces. However, many types of agro-food have curved surfaces, including tomatoes, apples, melons, and watermelons. Compared with reading QR codes on regular surfaces, reading QR codes attached to curved surfaces is challenging in terms of efficiency. The following parameters require further study: (1) how different conditions affect readability results, (2) whether a measurable model can be developed for ensuring that reading conditions correspond with results, and (3) determination of the optimal reading conditions for different agro-food types with varying degrees of curvature. To examine these parameters, we apply in this study a response surface methodology (RSM) to obtain the optimal reading parameters for curved agro-food. In addition, QR code readability is tested experimentally by using two typical fruits with curved surfaces.
Tracing systems
Tracing systems are fundamentally based on the following three factors: a product identification system, a supply chain management system, and a central database (Olsen & Borit, 2018). Two-dimensional barcodes have become an effective approach for product identification. In most applications, product labels containing 2D barcodes are printed by a barcode printer linked with a supply chain management system. The 2D barcode contains product information, including the production batch ID,

With nonoptimized parameters, the readability success rate is not high, which degrades the tracing experience for customers, and customer experience plays a vital role in the success of applications of tracing systems. We therefore use a RSM analysis to develop an optimization method for products with curved surfaces. The primary factors that significantly affect QR code readability include reading distance, ball diameter, the interaction between reading distance and code size, and the interaction between ball diameter and code size. MANUAL OF SPECIFICATIONS (MOP)
Synthetic GI Application Dataset Package
This literature-based synthetic document is designed for Geographical Indication (GI) research, IPOPHL application prototyping, academic studies, and system development. All records are synthetic but modeled from published sources and realistic Philippine coffee production conditions.
SECTION 1: IDENTIFICATION OF PRODUCT AND APPLICANT
GI Name: KAPENG BARAKO
Scientific Name: Coffea liberica W.Bull
Product Category: Agricultural Product – Coffee
Applicant Organization: Batangas-Cavite Liberica Producers Cooperative (Synthetic)
Region: CALABARZON, Philippines
SECTION 2: GEOGRAPHICAL AREA
Covered municipalities include Lipa City, Taal, Agoncillo, Lemery, Balayan, Calaca, Tagaytay City,
Silang, Amadeo, and nearby coffee-producing areas. Elevation ranges from 100–800 masl.
Climate is tropical with annual rainfall between 1,500–3,000 mm.
SECTION 3: PRODUCT DESCRIPTION
Kapeng Barako refers exclusively to Coffea liberica grown within the defined GI area.
Beans are large, asymmetrical, aromatic, and produce a bold cup profile characterized by floral,
fruit, chocolate, and smoky notes.
SECTION 4: LINK TO GEOGRAPHICAL ORIGIN
The product's reputation is linked to volcanic soils influenced by Taal Volcano,
favorable climate conditions, and more than two centuries of traditional cultivation.
SECTION 5: PRODUCTION METHODS
Cultivation follows agroforestry-based systems. Cherries are selectively hand-picked,
processed through washed or natural methods, sun-dried to ≤12% moisture, graded,
and roasted according to GI standards.
SECTION 6: QUALITY CONTROL
All lots undergo farm inspection, harvest verification, moisture testing,
defect analysis, and traceability validation.
SECTION 7: LABELING RULES
Labels must indicate GI name, origin, species, processing method,
lot number, producer information, and traceability code.
SECTION 8: CONTROL BODY
Synthetic model assumes inspections are performed by a cooperative quality committee,
LGU agriculture representatives, and accredited inspectors.
SECTION 9: HISTORY AND REPUTATION
Kapeng Barako has been cultivated in Batangas since the Spanish colonial period and remains
one of the Philippines' most recognized heritage coffee products.
SECTION 10: SCIENTIFIC REFERENCES
Compiled from publicly available literature on Coffea liberica morphology,
land suitability, volcanic soils, and Philippine coffee production.

Each lot is assigned a unique QR code linked to farm identity, harvest batch, processing lot, quality inspection record, and final packaged product.

Farm maps and GIS coordinates
LGU certifications

-INTE 302– Information Assurance and Security
Week 1: Introduction to Information Assurance
Information Assurance (IA) - refers to the protection of information systems against unauthorized access, modification, destruction, or disruption. It ensures that information remains reliable, secure, and usable.
	It includes policies, governance, risk management, and legal compliance
Cybersecurity focuses - mainly on protecting digital systems using technical controls such as firewalls and antivirus
Creating security policy + training employees = Information Assurance
The CIA Triad represents the three core principles of Information Assurance:
Confidentiality -ensures that information is accessible only to authorized    individuals.
Ex.
Password-protected LMS
Encrypted online banking transactions
Scenario: A professor accidentally shares grades publicly.
Answer: Confidentiality was violated because unauthorized disclosure occurred.
Integrity - ensures that information remains accurate and unaltered
Ex.
Digital signatures verify authenticity.
Hash values detect changes in files.
Scenario: A student alters grades in the system.
Answer: Integrity was violated due to unauthorized modification.
Availability - ensures that systems and data are accessible when needed.
Ex.
Backup servers
Disaster recovery plans
Scenario: A DDoS attack shuts down a website.
Answer: Availability was violated due to service disruption.
All security mechanisms aim to protect one or more of these principles
Weeks 2–3: Threats, Attacks, and Vulnerabilities
Threat – It is any potential cause of an unwanted incident that may harm a system.
	Examples:
Hacker attack
Malware infection
Insider misuse
Vulnerability – It is a weakness that can be exploited by a threat.
	Examples:
Weak passwords
Outdated software
Poor access control
Malware – It is malicious software designed to damage or disrupt systems.
                   	Common types:
Virus
Worm
Trojan
Ransomware
Spyware
Phishing - tricks users into revealing sensitive information
	Example:
Fake GCash email asking for login details.
Answer: Confidentiality is compromised when credentials are stolen
Insider Theat - originates from within the organization.
	Example:
Employee copying confidential data.
Answer: Confidentiality and possibly Integrity are violated.
OWASP - identifies the most critical web application security risks.
	Examples:
Injection attacks
Broken authentication
Sensitive data exposure
These represent common vulnerabilities exploited by attackers.
Cryptography and Network Security
Cryptography - It is the practice and study of techniques for secure communication in the presence of third parties.
The word cryptography comes from the two Greek words: Krypto (secret) and graphein (write).So cryptography means secret writing.
The art and science of keeping messages secure is called cryptography and it is practiced by cryptographers
Modern cryptography exists at the intersection of the disciplines of mathematics, computer science, and electrical engineering. Applications of cryptography include ATM cards, computer passwords, and electronic commerce.
History of Cryptography
50 B.C. - Julius Caesar uses cryptograp technique
400 A.D. - Kama Sutra in India mentions cryptographic techniques
1250 - British monk Roger Bacon describes simple ciphers
1466 - Leon Alberti develops a cipher disk
1861 - Union forces use a cipher during Civil War
1914- World War I – British, French, and German forces use encryption
technology
1917 - William Friedman, Father of U.S. encryption efforts starts a school for teaching cryptanalysis in Illinois
1917 - AT&T employee Gilbert Vernam invents polyalphabetic cipher
1919 - Germans develop the Engima machine for encryption
1937 - Japanese design the Purple machine for encryption
1942 - Navajo windtalkers help with secure communication during World War II
1948 - Claude Shannon develops statistical methods for encryption/decryption
1976 - IBM develops DES
1976 - Diffie – Hellman develop public key / private key cryptography
1977 - Rivest – Shamir – Adleman develop the RSA algorithm for public key / private key
Plaintext - is a text, in natural readable form. It is the message or data before it gets encrypted. In simple words it is the original message.
It is sometimes called clear text. Plaintext is denoted by M (message) or P (plaintext).
It can be a stream of bits, a text file, a bitmap, a stream of digitized voice etc.
Cipher text - It is the results obtained from the plaintext by applying the encryption algorithm on the plaintext.
An encrypted message is called cipher text. It is denoted by C (cipher text).
Cipher text is unreadable by anyone except the intended recipients
Encryption - The process of disguising a message in such a way to hide its substance is called encryption.
It is the process of scrambling a message using a specialized cryptographic algorithm to make it unreadable by anyone except the intended recipients.
The encryption function E, operates on M to produce C. In mathematical notation      E(M)=C
Plaintext = Hi buddy! -> Encryption -> Cipher text = blank.
Decryption - The process of converting cipher text back to the original plaintext.
Since the whole point of encrypting and then decrypting a message is to recover the original plaintext, the following identity must hold true:   D(E(M)) = M
Cipher text = D@#%^245 -> Decryption -> Plaintext = blank
Cryptanalysis - The art and science of breaking cipher text is called cryptanalysis
Cryptanalysis deals with finding the encryption key for breaking cryptographic algorithms without the knowledge of the encryption
Cryptanalyst: a person who breaks cryptographic codes. Also referred to as “the attacker” or the “intruder”.
Cryptology - Cryptography and cryptanalysis is collectively known as Cryptology.
The branch of mathematics encompasses both cryptography and cryptanalysis is called cryptology and its practitioners are called cryptologists.  
Modern cryptologists are generally trained in theoretical mathematics—they have to be.
Confidentiality Issues - It should be possible for the receiver of a message to ascertain its origin. An intruder should not be able to masquerade as someone else.
Confidentiality or Characteristics
Three confidentiality or characteristics of cryptography
Authentication: means that you know who created and sent the message. Digital signature is used to authenticate the source of messages. It ensures the sender of the message. 
Two solutions to ensure authentication are:
Passwords
Digital signatures
Integrity: means the message delivered to the receiver intact, without being changed or altered anything. Integrity is the assurance that the information is trustworthy and accurate. Digital signature ensures the integrity of message.
Technical solutions include:
Encryption
Hashing algorithms
Non-repudiation: this is an important criteria of digital signature. As digital signature ensures the authentication of the message, so the receiver can’t repudiate it later.  At the same time it also ensures the identity of the receiver, so the receiver can’t repudiate it later.
Cryptographic Algorithm - also called a cipher, is the mathematical function used for encryption and decryption.
Generally, there are two related functions: one for encryption and the other for decryption
Types of Cryptographic Algorithm
Symmetric Algorithm: it is also called Secret Key Cryptography (SKC). Uses a single key for both encryption and decryption
Asymmetric algorithm: it is also called Public Key Cryptography (PKC). Uses one key for encryption and another for decryption
Hash Functions: Uses a mathematical transformation to irreversibly "encrypt" information
Secret Key Cryptography - a single or same key is used for both encryption and decryption.  In some SKC, the encryption key is calculated from the decryption key and vice versa
Because a single key is used for both functions, secret key cryptography is also called symmetric encryption.
These algorithms, also called single key algorithms, or one-key algorithms. This algorithm requires the sender and receiver to agree on a unique key before they can communicate securely.
A wide variety of symmetric key algorithms are currently in use:
Data Encryption Standard (DES), 
Triple DES (3DES),
Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), 
Blowfish
CAST
International Data Encryption Algorithm (IDEA), 
Rivest Cipher (RC2, RC3, RC4, RC5, RC6) 
Steam cipher: it operates on the plaintext a single bits(or sometimes byte) at a time; these are called stream algorithms or stream ciphers
Block cipher: it operates on the plaintext in groups of bits. The groups of bits are called blocks, and the algorithms are called block algorithms or block ciphers. For modern computer algorithms, a typical block size is 64 bits—large enough to preclude analysis and small enough to be workable.
Public Key Cryptography - The concept Asymmetric Encryption (also known as Public Key Encryption) was devised in 1975 by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman and is based on the concept of using a pair of keys, one for encryption and one for decryption. The encryption key is often called the public key, and the decryption key is often called the private key
It is called "public-key cryptography" because the encryption key can be made public. A complete stranger can use the encryption key to encrypt a message, but only a specific person with the corresponding decryption key can decrypt the message

1. Application Form & Applicant Details 
Name of Applicant Organization:​
Lipa City Kapeng Barako Producers Association (Sample) 
Type of Applicant:​
Association of Coffee Producers

Juan Dela Cruz​
President, Lipa City Kapeng Barako Producers Association 
Contact Information:​
Email: info@kapengbarakolipa.ph​
Contact Number: +63 9095405923 
 
2. Geographical Indication Name 
Proposed Geographical Indication (GI):​
"KAPENG BARAKO NG LIPA" 
Alternative Name:​
"Lipa Kapeng Barako" 
Product Category:​
Agricultural Product – Coffee Beans 
Scientific Name:​
Coffea liberica 
 
3. Product Description 
Kapeng Barako ng Lipa is a premium Liberica coffee grown within the territorial boundaries of 
Lipa City, Batangas. The coffee is recognized for its strong aroma, bold flavor profile, naturally 
high caffeine content, and distinct fruity and floral notes. 
The beans are larger than those of Arabica and Robusta varieties and possess unique sensory 
characteristics that have established Kapeng Barako as one of the most culturally significant 
coffee products in the Philippines. 
Distinct characteristics include: 
• Large bean size​
• Strong and intense aroma​

• Full-bodied flavor​
• Low acidity​
• Fruity and floral undertones​
• Traditional cultivation methods practiced by local farmers 
The reputation of Kapeng Barako has been established through generations of production and 
consumption in Batangas Province, particularly in Lipa City. 
 
4. Geographical Area Description 
The geographical area covered by this application consists exclusively of Lipa City, Batangas, 
Philippines. 
Geographical Coordinates:​
Approximately 13.94° N Latitude and 121.16° E Longitude 
Boundaries: 
North: Municipality of Cuenca​
South: Municipality of San Jose​
East: Municipality of Mataas na Kahoy​
West: Municipality of Malvar 
The area is characterized by: 
• Volcanic soil influenced by Taal Volcano​
• Elevation ranging from 100–400 meters above sea level​
• Tropical climate with distinct wet and dry seasons​
• Average annual rainfall suitable for Liberica coffee cultivation 
These environmental conditions contribute significantly to the quality and distinctive 
characteristics of Kapeng Barako grown in Lipa City. 
5. Product Specification Manual 
A. Raw Material 
Species: Coffea liberica 
Source: Coffee trees cultivated exclusively within Lipa City. 
 
B. Cultivation Standards 
1.​ Coffee trees must be planted within the designated geographical area. 
2.​ Farmers shall maintain good agricultural practices. 
3.​ Organic and sustainable farming methods are encouraged. 
4.​ Farm records shall be maintained for traceability purposes. 
C. Harvesting Standards 
1.​ Only mature red coffee cherries shall be harvested. 
2.​ Selective hand-picking shall be practiced. 

3.​ Immature and damaged cherries shall be excluded. 
 
D. Processing Standards 
1.​ Cherries shall be processed within 24 hours after harvesting. 
2.​ Drying shall achieve moisture content between 10–12%. 
3.​ Sorting and grading shall remove defective beans. 
4.​ Storage shall protect beans from moisture contamination. 
 
E. Quality Requirements 
Physical Characteristics: 
• Large bean size​
• Uniform appearance​
• Moisture content not exceeding 12% 
Sensory Characteristics: 
• Strong aroma​
• Full-bodied taste​
• Distinct floral and fruity notes​
• Minimal bitterness​
• Low acidity 
 
6. Evidence of Link Between Product and 
Geographical Origin 
Historical Evidence 
Lipa City became the center of the Philippine coffee industry during the nineteenth century. 
Historical records indicate that Batangas, particularly Lipa, achieved international recognition for 
its coffee production and export activities. 
Cultural Evidence 
Kapeng Barako has become an integral part of Batangueño identity and heritage. Traditional 
cultivation and processing practices have been transmitted across generations of farming 
families. 
Environmental Evidence 
The volcanic soil composition, elevation, rainfall patterns, and climate conditions of Lipa City 
contribute directly to the flavor, aroma, and quality characteristics of Kapeng Barako. 
Scientific Evidence 

Agricultural studies indicate that the environmental conditions present in Batangas support the 
cultivation of high-quality Coffea liberica. The interaction between soil composition, climate, and 
farming practices influences bean development and sensory attributes. 
Market Reputation 
Kapeng Barako is widely recognized by consumers, traders, and tourism stakeholders as a 
distinctive coffee product associated with Lipa City and Batangas Province. 
 
7. Inspection and Traceability System 
The producer association shall maintain a traceability and verification system to ensure 
compliance with GI standards. 
The system shall include: 
• Farmer registration records​
• Farm location verification​
• Production records​
• Harvest monitoring records​
• Batch identification numbers​
• QR code-based traceability mechanism​
• Product verification reports 
 
8. Certification Request 
The applicant respectfully requests the registration of "KAPENG BARAKO NG LIPA" as a 
Geographical Indication under applicable Philippine laws and regulations governing 
Geographical Indications. 
The applicant certifies that the product possesses qualities, characteristics, and reputation 
essentially attributable to its geographical origin and that all information submitted in this 
application is true and correct.

Technical Specifications outline the exact chemical, biological, and physical parameters that the 
agricultural product must satisfy to qualify for official certification and quality assurance. This 
includes detailed metrics regarding maximum moisture content, allowable size variations of the 
harvested goods, and strict limits on chemical residues or defects per batch. Maintaining these 
rigorous technical baselines guarantees a uniform standard of excellence, ensuring that every 
certified item leaving the production facility meets the expectations of premium commercial 
markets. 
 
PROOF LINK

agricultural product and the distinct geographical environment where it is cultivated. This section 
provides scientific data and historical documentation demonstrating how the unique soil 
composition, microclimate, and local farming traditions directly create the characteristic flavor, 
aroma, or texture of the harvest. Without establishing this undeniable environmental connection, 
a product cannot legally claim geographic exclusivity or be protected against generic market 
imitations. 
 
APPLICANT ELIGIBILITY 
Applicant Eligibility defines the specific criteria, legal status, and organizational structures that a 
group or entity must possess to formally file for product protection. This requirement stipulates 
that individual farmers, processors, or agricultural cooperatives must be legally registered and 
actively operating within the designated boundary to participate in the application. Documenting 
this eligibility ensures that the rights to the protected name belong collectively to the genuine 
local community and cannot be monopolized or exploited by outside commercial entities. 
 
EVIDENCE OF REPUTATION 
Evidence of Reputation comprises historical texts, market data, awards, and media publications 
that officially document the long-standing public recognition and commercial value of the 
agricultural product. This dossier serves as historical proof that the product’s exceptional status is 
not a recent marketing trend, but a well-established legacy built over decades or centuries of 
trade and consumer appreciation. Providing this verified track record justifies the need for legal 
protection, demonstrating that the name holds significant cultural and economic value worth 
safeguarding.

Inspection designates the independent, accredited authority responsible for conducting regular 
audits, field checks, and laboratory testing to verify strict compliance with established production 
standards. This regulatory entity monitors the entire supply chain—from the initial planting and 
harvesting phases to processing, packaging, and distribution—to prevent fraud and maintain 
consumer trust. By enforcing unbiased quality control, this organization ensures that all

MANUAL OF SPECIFICATIONS FOR THE GEOGRAPHICAL INDICATION
LIPA KAPENG BARAKO
(Coffea liberica W.Bull)

COMPLETED DATASET NOTICE: This version contains verified empirical metrics, synthetic lab configurations, and local cooperative frameworks mapping directly to the 'FIELD DATA NEEDED' gaps of general regional templates. It serves as a fully populated model for IPOPHL evaluation under Memorandum Circular No. 2022-022.
SECTION 1: IDENTIFICATION OF THE PRODUCT AND APPLICANT
SECTION 2: DESCRIPTION OF THE GEOGRAPHICAL AREA
2.1 Delineated Production Zone
The geographical zone unique to Lipa Kapeng Barako is localized strictly within the historical coffee-producing micro-climate of Lipa City, Batangas, Philippines. Situated on a high-altitude inland volcanic plateau surrounding the Taal caldera basin, production is anchored across agricultural areas within the administrative boundaries of Lipa City, focusing intensely on the prime high-altitude coffee-belts of Barangays Lodlod, Mataasnakahoy boundary corridors, Marawoy, Pinagkawitan, Sabang, and Balintawak. This area represents the continuous historical heartland of Coffea liberica commercial cultivation since its introduction in the 18th century.
Table 2.1: Micro-Climate and Terrane Parameters of the Delineated Zone
2.2 Geological and Volcanic Soil Character
The defining physical element of Lipa City's terroir is its placement on deep layers of the Lipa Soil Series—a subset of volcanic Andisols originating directly from ancient explosive cycles of the neighboring Taal Volcano framework. These soils possess exceptionally high natural macro-porosity and rapid hydraulic drainage properties. The physical matrix is packed with high active concentrations of total exchangeable Potassium (K), available Phosphorus (P), and vital micronutrients (Boron, Iron, and Zinc), linked to unique cation exchange capacities driven by amorphous clay structures like allophane (Mihai et al., 2023). This mineral configuration allows deep root penetration for the tree, transferring an assertive nutrient payload that accelerates high metabolic concentration in developing coffee embryos.
SECTION 3: DESCRIPTION OF THE PRODUCT
3.1 Botanical Identity and General Description
Lipa Kapeng Barako consists strictly of 100% pure green, roasted, or ground coffee beans derived exclusively from the botanical species Coffea liberica W.Bull (Family Rubiaceae). The tree architecture is notably mega-phytic, reaching heights up to 20 meters in old un-pruned agroforest locations, showcasing high resistance to drought and local pathogens like coffee leaf rust (Hemileia vastatrix). The beans exhibit an expressive, highly asymmetrical structure where the proximal end finishes in a distinct curve or hook, split by a deeply complex, jagged center furrow.
Table 3.1: Morphometric Parameters of Lipa Coffea liberica Frameworks
3.2 Empirical Sensory and Chemical Composition Metrics
• Official Q-Grader Cupping Score: 84.75 Points (Classified as Fine Specialty Grade Liberica under SCA Protocols).
• Sensory Flavor Matrix: Pungent ripe jackfruit, dark baker's chocolate, star anise, toasted molasses, muscovado sugar back-notes, with a dense, silky, heavy mouthfeel and an extraordinarily persistent sweet-woody aftertaste.
• Caffeine Concentration: 1.18% (Dry-matter basis; naturally lower than robusta, providing clean clarity with rich density).
• Total Chlorogenic Acids (CGA): 3.42% (Contributing to a smooth finish with minimized astringency).
• Total Soluble Solids (TSS): 5.8° Brix (Reflecting complex mucilage carbohydrate development during ripening).
SECTION 4: LINK BETWEEN THE PRODUCT AND ITS GEOGRAPHICAL ORIGIN
4.1 Natural Factors Interaction
The unique bold character of Lipa Kapeng Barako is directly derived from a structural confluence of geography and soil kinetics. The high altitude inland plateau of Lipa City provides cool evening ambient air blocks which slows down cellular division inside the ripening fruit. This delayed maturity allows the extensive leaf area (mean 308.74 cm²) to perform prolonged photosynthetic carbohydrate synthesis. These sugars migrate heavily into the expansive bean volume (mean 2,832.91 mm³), fueled by the high-cation soil matrix of volcanic Andisols. Additionally, the intercropped agroforestry system provides natural partial shade from native fruit trees, preventing thermal shock on the fruit clusters.

4.2 Human and Historical Factors
Lipa City's identity has been fundamentally linked to the coffee trade since 1740 when Spanish Franciscans planted the first seeds. By the 1880s, Lipa became the global sole supplier of premium coffee during the peak of Europe's leaf rust outbreak, generating massive historical wealth. Generations of Lipangueño farmers developed 'Pagpupunla and Pagpili'—a systematic selective picking methodology. Furthermore, the local culinary tradition of using concentrated Barako brew as a savory 'sabaw' (pour-over soup broth) over dried lake fish like tawilis or tapa showcases a unique socio-cultural integration that maintains strict localized processing standards.
SECTION 5: PRODUCTION METHODS AND STANDARDS
5.1 Standard Cultivation Requirements
• Planting Density Matrix: Strictly 1,111 trees per hectare configured in a 3.0m x 3.0m square grid layout. Intercropping requires a minimum of 20% shade coverage provided by alternating rows of Gliricidia sepium, Artocarpus heterophyllus (Jackfruit), or Cocos nucifera.
• Nutrient Management: Soil must be augmented using aged organic compost or decomposed coffee cherry pulp at 5 kg/tree/year, keeping soil pH strictly between 5.5 and 6.5.
• Harvest Windows and Rules: Harvest is strictly limited to the peak season window from November 15 to February 28. Strip-harvesting is totally banned. Farmers must selectively hand-pick only fully mature deep-red cherries showing a minimum of 90% pigment saturation across the cluster.
5.2 Post-Harvest Processing Specifications
• Traditional Wet Method (Standard): Cherries are float-sorted within 4 hours of picking. Mechanical or manual pulping is followed by controlled dry fermentation for 18 to 24 hours to break down complex mucilage. Beans must be washed thoroughly with potable spring or deep-well water.
• Solar Drying Regime: Beans must be spread on raised bamboo or mesh drying beds. Ground-drying on bare concrete is strictly prohibited. The drying process proceeds for 10–14 days until bean internal moisture stabilizes precisely at 11.0% to 12.0%.
• Master Roasting Curves: Roasting must occur inside the delineated city boundaries. The verified master curve dictates a charge temperature of 195°C, a slow medium-dark roast profile spanning exactly 14 minutes and 22 seconds, with a Development Time Ratio (DTR) of 18.5% to optimize deep essential oil migration without structural charring.
SECTION 6: LABELING, PACKAGING, AND TRACEABILITY CONTROL
6.1 Traceability Matrix
Every single package distributed under the GI registration must display a structured alphanumeric tracing code formatted as: LIPA-BARAKO-[FARM_ID]-[LOT_YEAR]. All lots must cross-reference back to the LCCGMC Central Ledger tracking farm coordinates, moisture curves, and Q-grader evaluation dates.

6.2 Packaging Architecture
Green Coffee Beans (GCB) must be stored and shipped in high-density multi-layer hermetic bags (e.g., GrainPro) wrapped in premium 300 GSM food-grade jute sacks. Roasted or ground variants must be vacuum-sealed immediately inside multi-layer aluminum foil pouches equipped with a integrated one-way degassing valve. The official embossed IPOPHL GI Protection Seal must be placed across the primary front closure panel.

This synthetic dataset was designed to mirror the type of stakeholder consultation evidence
commonly required during Geographical Indication (GI) preparation and registration processes. The
records are based on publicly available information regarding Kapeng Barako (Coffea liberica), GI

participation, traceability systems, quality control requirements, and consensus-building
mechanisms.

Consultation ID: SC-001
Date: 2025 Consultation Cycle
Stakeholder Group: Coffee Farmers, LGU Representatives, Traders, Roasters, Cooperatives,
Academic Experts, and Industry Organizations.
Participants: 21 attendees.
Primary Agenda: Delimitation of production area, producer registration, traceability, quality
standards, governance formation, Manual of Specifications (MoP), sustainability practices, market
protection, and GI compliance.
Discussion Summary: Participants discussed preserving the reputation of authentic Kapeng

name, inconsistent quality standards, insufficient farm documentation, counterfeit products, weak
supply-chain transparency, and the need for stronger producer representation. Stakeholders
recommended standardized farm records, harvest monitoring, QR-based traceability, sensory
evaluation protocols, producer accreditation, annual audits, and a formal GI governing council.

Beanthentic: A Random Forest–Driven and QR Code–Based Coffee Farmer Profiling System for Geographical Indication Recognition Readiness




A Capstone Project
Presented to the Faculty of the Information Technology
Polytechnic University of the Philippines - Sto. Tomas Campus
Sto. Tomas Batangas




In Partial Fulfillment of the Requirements for the Program
Bachelor of Science in Information Technology




by


BALAOGAN, NYCO ALEC B.
LAPITAN, REYMARC M.
MALIBIRAN, ELIAZA MAE C.
MAYNETE, ERICKA A.
RUBIA, MA. KRISHA N.
UMALI, KAZYRA M.





Month 202-


Chapter 1

THE PROBLEM AND ITS BACKGROUND



Introduction

	Coffee serves as a primary source of daily energy for many Filipino people; however, the coffee industry in the Philippines has been experiencing a gradual decline due to limited technological adoption and insufficient product recognition. One community significantly affected by this is the Kapeng Barako farmers in Lipa City, a place historically known as a center of Kapeng Barako production. This coffee variety, commonly associated with Liberica, alongside Robusta and Excelsa, holds not only economic value but also cultural importance. Over time, Kapeng Barako has become a symbol of strength, hospitality, and local identity, with roots tracing back to the 18th-century coffee boom in the region and continuing through periods of decline and revival (Buenaflor, 2025).
Despite its cultural and economic significance, Lipa City faces challenges in protecting and promoting Kapeng Barako. One key solution is obtaining a Geographical Indication (GI) seal, a legally recognized mechanism that protects the identity, quality, and origin of products by linking them to a specific geographic area. Established under the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIFS) in 1994, GI systems have been widely used to support rural development, preserve cultural heritage, and enhance market competitiveness (Cei et al., 2018). In the Philippines, the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL) is responsible for administering GI protection and promoting regionally significant products.
However, the process of obtaining GI certification is complex and time-consuming. It requires detailed documentation that proves the connection between product quality and geographic origin, as well as consistent production standards and reliable records. For many small-scale farmers, the financial cost and administrative requirements present significant challenges (Crespo-Moncada et al., 2025). These difficulties are further compounded by limited institutional support, making it harder for farmers to comply with GI requirements using traditional methods.
In addition, current documentation practices among Kapeng Barako farmers in Lipa City remain fragmented. Many farmers and cooperatives rely on individually maintained spreadsheets, with no centralized system to organize or integrate data across different barangays. Important information such as farmer profiles, harvest volumes, production inputs, and sales records are often inconsistent and incomplete. As a result, it becomes difficult to produce accurate, standardized, and verifiable data needed for GI certification. This lack of organized records not only delays the certification process but also limits transparency, which may affect fair pricing and market opportunities for farmers.
While modern agricultural technologies have improved areas such as crop monitoring and yield prediction, they often do not address the need for proper documentation required in certification processes (Deng et al., 2024; ScienceDirect, 2024). This highlights a significant gap: farming communities aiming for GI recognition lack accessible tools that can help them systematically manage records and meet regulatory requirements.
To address this gap, this study proposes Beanthentic, a centralized farmer profiling system designed to support record management and production monitoring. The system aims to simplify record-keeping by organizing production data and improving accessibility of information. It also incorporates a Random Forest–based model to assist in assessing farmers’ readiness for Geographical Indication (GI) certification based on established standards. Through these features, the system seeks to support coffee farmers in Lipa City in their efforts to achieve GI recognition and strengthen the value of Kapeng Barako.

 Project Context 
Beanthentic is a farmer profiling system supported by a Random Forest–based model, developed to enhance and streamline the Geographical Indication (GI) certification process for coffee producers in Lipa City. The system serves as a centralized digital platform that consolidates, standardizes, and organizes comprehensive farmer data into a unified profiling framework. It also manages transactional updates, such as tracking production yield and deducting sales, to ensure accurate inventory monitoring for every harvest season. Through this, the system promotes transparency, accuracy, and data security among farmers. By integrating all registered coffee farmers into a structured and validated system, Beanthentic establishes a reliable foundation for assessing the GI readiness of Kapeng Barako in Lipa City.
To further strengthen transparency and supply chain traceability, Beanthentic incorporates QR code technology linked directly to each authenticated farmer’s digital profile. These QR codes provide authorized users, including consumers, access to see verified information on production per harvest season. This feature supports transparency in product origin and enables farmers to build trust in the market. In addition, the system includes safeguards to prevent misuse or misconduct of information. Overall, this QR-enabled traceability mechanism enhances accountability, reduces information gaps, and fosters trust among farmers and consumers in the market.
Furthermore, the system integrates a Random Forest–based model that assists in evaluating whether Lipa City meets the necessary criteria for obtaining a Geographical Indication (GI) seal. This evaluation feature is embedded within the administrative panel of Beanthentic, where only authorized administrators can input and manage the required documentation. This controlled access ensures data security and aligns with the requirements set by the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines, where only qualified members are permitted to submit GI-related documents.
Given the complexity and one-time nature of the GI application process, the Random Forest model was developed using a scientific evidence synthesis approach. This method involves combining insights from multiple academic studies and established GI documentation standards to identify key indicators required for certification. The model is based on criteria provided by IPOPHL and supported by relevant literature. The use of synthesized data is appropriate due to the unique characteristics of Kapeng Barako, including its specific production practices and environmental conditions. In future implementation, as Lipa City progresses in its GI application, real data can be incorporated into the system to further see the potential and accuracy of assessments. This approach can help reduce both the time and cost required for evaluating GI readiness while providing meaningful insights for decision-making.
Beanthentic addresses a critical need at the intersection of agricultural governance, intellectual property, and supply chain transparency. For farmers, the system provides a structured and validated platform that supports their participation in the Geographical Indication (GI) process. Additionally, QR-enabled traceability enhances confidence in the authenticity of Kapeng Barako products among consumers and market stakeholders. The system also offers a more efficient alternative to traditionally manual and resource-intensive evaluation processes. In the context of GI development efforts in the Philippines, Beanthentic presents a potential model that can be adapted by other agricultural communities seeking formal recognition for their region-specific products.

 Theoretical Framework
This study is based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) developed by Fred Davis in 1989, which explains how users come to accept and use new technologies. TAM posits that system adoption is primarily influenced by two key beliefs: Perceived Usefulness (PU), or the degree to which users believe the system enhances their performance, and Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU), or the degree to which users believe the system requires minimal effort. These beliefs shape users’ behavioral intentions and ultimately their actual system usage. In the context of the proposed centralized profiling system supporting Geographical Indication (GI) documentation readiness for Kapeng Barako in Lipa City, Batangas, TAM provides a framework for assessing whether coffee farmers perceive the system as beneficial, practical, and easy to operate for improving data management and traceability.
      The study also adopts the ISO/IEC 25010 developed by the International Organization for Standardization to evaluate the overall quality of the system. This model defines internationally recognized software quality characteristics, including functional suitability, performance efficiency, usability, reliability, security, and portability, which serve as benchmarks for assessing whether the system performs its profiling and monitoring functions accurately, operates efficiently, protects sensitive data, and remains stable for continuous use. By integrating TAM and ISO/IEC 25010, the study ensures that the system is both technically sound and acceptable to its intended users, thereby strengthening its effectiveness in supporting GI documentation processes.

Scope and Limitation of the Study 
	This study covers the development and evaluation of Beanthentic, a centralized farmer profiling system designed to support the Geographical Indication (GI) documentation readiness of Kapeng Barako in Lipa City, Batangas. The system encompasses four primary functional areas: centralized farmer profiling, production monitoring, QR-based traceability, and a Random Forest AI-driven GI readiness assessment aligned with IPOPHL standards. The centralized profiling component consolidates and standardizes coffee farmer information across registered barangays into a unified system, while the production monitoring feature enables systematic tracking of harvest yields and sales transactions per season. The QR-based traceability mechanism links each authenticated farmer's profile to a unique QR code, allowing authorized users and consumers to access verified production information and supporting transparency in product origin. The system operates on two platforms: a mobile application for farmers and a web application for administrators. 
The system is developed exclusively for the coffee farming community of Lipa City, Batangas, with a specific focus on Kapeng Barako, and is not intended for use in other regions or agricultural products without significant modifications. Beanthentic functions solely as an assistive tool and does not hold or replace any authority vested in IPOPHL. The GI certification process remains under the full jurisdiction of IPOPHL, and the system is intended only to help streamline preliminary documentation and reduce associated costs, not to substitute the legal and regulatory requirements of the actual application process. Additionally, the study does not involve any financial transactions or monetary collection from farmers, as the system is entirely non-commercial in nature. All production and sales transactions recorded in the system are solely the responsibility of the farmers themselves, and any falsification of inputs falls outside the scope of the system's accountability.
The accuracy and completeness of data within the system are dependent on the cooperation and honesty of the farmers and cooperatives who input their records, as prior documentation practices in the community were fragmented and inconsistent. The Random Forest model was developed using a scientific evidence synthesis approach drawn from academic literature and established IPOPHL GI standards, given the absence of actual GI application data for Kapeng Barako. As a result, the model's predictive accuracy has not yet been validated against real-world outcomes, and future integration of actual application data will be necessary to further refine its performance. Furthermore, the effective use of the system is subject to hardware and software requirements, including a stable internet connection, sufficient device storage, capable smartphone specifications for farmers, and appropriate computer specifications for administrators. Limited digital literacy among small-scale farmers and inadequate access to devices or connectivity may also affect the adoption and full utilization of the system.

Geographical Indications and Legal Frameworks for Agricultural Products
      According to Almusawir et al. (2025), Geographical Indications (GIs) are protected under national and international legal frameworks, particularly the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) and Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL), which aims to safeguard agricultural products whose quality and reputation are linked to their place of origin. Their study emphasizes that GI protection prevents product misrepresentation, strengthens producer rights, and preserves the authenticity of region-based agricultural goods.
        Similarly, Hofmeier et al. (2023) examined the adoption of Geographical Indications among small and medium-sized enterprises and highlighted the importance of clear legal structures and institutional support in effective GI implementation. The authors noted that despite the availability of legal protection, GI adoption is often constrained by complex registration procedures, limited awareness among producers, and weak enforcement mechanisms.
       In the context of agri-food supply chains, Rackl and Menapace (2024) explained that Geographical Indication certification functions as a legally recognized quality signal that reduces information asymmetry between producers and consumers. Their findings show that GI frameworks can enhance coordination and trust within supply chains; however, their effectiveness depends on reliable verification and monitoring systems.
     Likewise, Li and Ouyang (2025) investigated the socio-economic impacts of GI certification and found that legally protected GIs contribute to improved farmer income, market access, and overall well-being. The study also pointed out that these benefits are lessened when governance structures are weak and when traceability and compliance mechanisms are insufficient.
       Finally, the Department of Trade and Industry (2025) documented the recognition of Guimaras mangoes as the Philippines’ first officially registered Geographical Indication product. Geographical Indication Recognition and Documentation Readiness
According to Silva et al. (2023), major coffee-producing countries such as Brazil, Vietnam, Colombia, and Indonesia utilize Geographical Indications (GIs) to protect and differentiate their coffee in the global market. Their bibliographical and documental analysis showed that GI protection is implemented either through specific legislation or trademark systems, with Brazil recognizing Indication of Origin (IO) and Denomination of Origin (DO). The study highlights the importance of strong legal frameworks and institutional support in sustaining GI protection.
Furthermore, Juwita et al. (2025) conducted a bibliometric analysis of GI coffee research to identify trends, leading journals, top contributing countries, and thematic focuses. Their review of Scopus-indexed publications from 2003–2024 revealed a notable increase in GI coffee research after 2016, peaking in 2022, with Italy and the Slovak University of Agriculture as top contributors. Recent studies emphasized chemometrics, adulteration, and food quality, highlighting opportunities for integrating digital systems, traceability, and proper documentation. These bibliometric findings reinforce the importance of systematic GI recognition and documentation readiness to support future research and ensure product authenticity.
In addition, Barjolle et al. (2017) analyzed the role of the state in implementing and managing GIs in the coffee sectors of Colombia and Kenya. Their comparative case study showed that GI recognition and documentation require active governance, including legal protection, quality control, and institutional coordination between public authorities and private actors. The study highlights that legal registration alone is insufficient; effective management, collective action, and flexible state involvement are crucial to ensure that GI benefits reach producers. These insights underscore that structured GI recognition and documentation systems are key to maintaining authenticity, supporting value creation, and empowering coffee producers.
Moreover, Artêncio et al. (2021) investigated the influence of Geographical Indication (GI) labeling on consumer perception and preference during coffee tasting, including unconscious neural responses measured via EEG. Their experiment with 40 participants compared GI and non-GI labeled coffee samples and analyzed neural responses across multiple brain waves. The study found that GI labeling significantly influenced consumer responses, with women showing broader sensitivity to GI cues than men. EEG results indicated men preferred GI-labeled coffee, while women’s preferences were less consistent between neural responses and verbal reporting. Overall, GI labeling acts as a strong extrinsic cue affecting perception and expectation, highlighting its value as a marketing tool and the need to integrate neuromarketing insights into consumer education and traceability awareness.
Lastly, the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI, 2025) announced the recognition of Guimaras mangoes as the first Philippine product granted Geographical Indication (GI) status. This official recognition ensures legal protection against imitation, strengthens consumer trust, and positions the product alongside internationally recognized GI goods. The GI status is expected to increase market value, protect cultural heritage, and improve farmer livelihoods. DTI also encourages continued capacity building for farmers, wider promotion of the GI seal, expansion of domestic and international market access, and stronger consumer awareness campaigns to maximize the benefits of GI recognition.
