RESEARCH METHODOLOGY


This chapter presents the key research elements namely: research methods used, the population and sample size, the research instrument, the data gathering procedure and the statistical treatments of the data. It also provides discussions of the methods to be used in developing the system output of the study.

Research Method & Participants 
This study utilizes a descriptive-quantitative research method to evaluate the technical performance and user acceptance of the system. As a descriptive study, it systematically characterizes the system's alignment with the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality standards and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) through numerical data. This approach allows the researchers to transform subjective experiences into objective, statistical evidence, providing a clear basis for determining the system’s effectiveness in coffee farmer profiling to support Geographic Indication (GI) readiness assessment in Lipa City.
The participants of the study consist of fifty (50) coffee farmers in Lipa City, Batangas, selected through purposive sampling to ensure the collection of relevant data from the primary end-users. The sample size of 50 participants was considered sufficient to obtain reliable and meaningful evaluation results while remaining manageable within the study’s time and resource constraints. The selected participants share common characteristics, including active involvement in coffee farming, engagement in the production and sale of coffee beans, and residency within the designated geographical area of Lipa City. As primary stakeholders, these farmers are responsible for evaluating the system’s usability, practical utility, and overall quality in a real-world agricultural context.
Research Instrument
The study utilizes a structured research questionnaire as the primary instrument for evaluating the Beanthentic system. The questionnaire is designed to quantitatively assess both the software quality and user acceptance centralized coffee farmer profiling system. To ensure a comprehensive evaluation, the instrument is grounded in two established frameworks: the ISO/IEC 25010 Software Quality Model and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). By integrating these models, the instrument captures both the system’s technical performance and its practical viability for users in the agricultural sector of Lipa City, Batangas.	
The questionnaire is divided into two primary sections, both administered to the participating coffee farmers. The first section focuses on user acceptance based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), measuring the key constructs of Perceived Usefulness defined as the system’s effectiveness in managing farmers’ profiling information in support of Kapeng Barako Geographic Indication (GI) readiness assessment and Perceived Ease of Use, which refers to how easily farmers can navigate and utilize the profiling features in their daily activities.
The second section is based on the ISO/IEC 25010 model and evaluates the system’s software quality characteristics from the users’ perspective. This includes assessing functional suitability, particularly the consistency and accuracy of the Random Forest algorithm in determining GI readiness in Lipa City; performance efficiency, especially in relation to the QR code–based features used in managing farmer profiles; the reliability of the profiling database,  as well as the system’s security and portability.
All items in the instrument are close-ended and quantitative, utilizing a five-point Likert scale to encourage more definitive responses and reduce neutral bias. To ensure clarity and inclusivity for the coffee farmers, the questionnaire is presented in a bilingual format, with Tagalog translations provided alongside the English technical terms.

Data Gathering Procedures 
The data gathering procedure for this study was conducted in systematic phases to ensure the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of the collected data. Prior to data collection, ethical clearance was secured from the appropriate research ethics review body. Informed consent forms were prepared and distributed to all participants, clearly explaining the purpose of the study, the voluntary nature of participation, the confidentiality of responses, and the participants’ right to withdraw at any time without any consequences.
The researchers conducted in-person data collection, assisting participants strictly with technical registration procedures such as account creation and system navigation within the Beanthentic platform. Each farmer created an account linked to a unique QR code, and their profiling data was recorded to support documentation for GI readiness. It is important to note that the researchers limited their role to technical assistance only and did not influence or interfere with any participant responses. All questionnaire responses were accomplished independently by the participants. After registration, the data were automatically received on the admin side of the system for monitoring and management of registered participants. 
Following the profiling process, a paper-based survey questionnaire was administered. The researchers demonstrated the system and guided participants through its features prior to answering. All completed questionnaires were checked, organized, and encoded for statistical analysis to ensure that the collected farmer profiling data and evaluation responses were accurate, reliable, and aligned with Beanthentic’s role as a centralized profiling and Random Forest AI based to support GI documentation.

System Development Methodology 






Figure 2. Agile Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) Model
	This study adopted the Agile Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) Model in developing Beanthentic. Agile was selected to enable iterative development, continuous refinement, and regular user feedback, ensuring that the system effectively meets the needs of coffee farmers and stakeholders, particularly the “Samahan ng Magkakape ng Lipa” and IPOPHL Calamba Office. 

Requirements Phase
	System requirements were identified through interviews and meetings with the Samahan ng Magkakape ng Lipa and IPOPHL Calamba, along with field observations and review of existing GI guidelines. 
Based on this phase, the core system components were defined:
Centralized digital coffee farmer profiling
Random Forest–based GI compliance pattern analysis
QR code–enabled traceability of farmer profiles
User-friendly web and mobile-accessible interfaces
	These requirements aimed to address fragmented farmer records and limited documentation systems supporting GI recognition readiness.
Design Phase
	Architectural planning was conducted using diagrams and system flowcharts. The design process also included the development of the system’s UI/UX using Figma to ensure a user-friendly and intuitive interface. 
Development Phase
	The development of Beanthentic was carried out in iterative sprints, enabling incremental backend, database, and frontend implementation with continuous refinements.
Key processes for the Random Forest algorithm included:
Data cleaning and validation
Encoding categorical variables
Splitting datasets into training and testing sets
Model training and evaluation based on GI readiness indicators
	QR codes were integrated to link each farmer profile with a unique scannable identifier, supporting traceability and organized GI documentation readiness.
Testing Phase
	System quality was evaluated using the ISO/IEC 25010 Software Quality Model, measuring:
Functional Suitability
Performance Efficiency
Reliability and Security
Portability
	User acceptance was assessed using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), focusing on Perceived Usefulness and Perceived Ease of Use among intended users.
	The Random Forest AI was tested using GI documentation datasets to ensure it correctly supports the profiling and GI readiness assessment processes, providing reliable guidance for decision-making and traceability within the system. 
Deployment Phase
	After testing and refinement, Beanthentic was deployed in a testing environment, accessible via a web-based administrative panel and a mobile application for farmers. The deployment allowed users to interact with the system for farmer profiling, submit and manage supporting documents, support GI readiness assessment, and utilize QR-code–enabled traceability for improved data management and verification. 
Maintenance Phase
	The Maintenance Phase ensures the continued reliability and relevance of Beanthentic by addressing system updates and enhancements. This includes fixing bugs, and improving usability and performance based on user feedback.

Systems Designs

Flowchart 
	

Figure 3.  Flowchart of Beanthentic System


This flowchart illustrates how the system operates, beginning with the client-side flow, where a user enters the application through a start screen, proceeds to a tutorial and login page, and chooses whether to sign up or log in. During registration, the user inputs personal details, submits requirements, and waits for approval before accessing the home page. Once inside, the user can navigate different features such as messaging, transactions, profile viewing, and history tracking. The flow also includes conditional paths where the user decides actions like sending messages, viewing notifications, or accessing transaction records, with each choice leading to corresponding pages such as receipts, transaction details, or history logs. 
On the admin side, the process focuses on system management and verification. The admin logs in through a secure page and gains access to a dashboard where they can manage users, review registrations, verify documents, and handle transactions. Decision points allow the admin to approve or reject accounts, monitor activities, and update system data such as posts, messages, and user information. The admin also oversees reporting and history tracking, ensuring that all user actions and transactions are properly recorded. Overall, the flowchart shows a structured interaction between client and admin, emphasizing authentication, data validation, and smooth navigation across features


















Use-Cases Diagrams































Figure 4. Use Case Diagram of Beanthentic System

The diagram shows the structured interaction between the Farmer and the Admin within the Brewthentic system, emphasizing controlled data submission and verification. On the farmer's side, the process begins with account registration and login, followed by language selection and viewing of system instructions to ensure proper guidance. The farmer then inputs detailed and categorized information, including personal details, farm information, farm affiliation, and production data. These inputs are essential components included in the submission for verification. The system allows the farmer to edit and review their profile before final submission, promoting accuracy and completeness. Once submitted, the farmer waits for verification and receives notifications regarding approval or required corrections. Upon approval, the farmer can generate and view a QR code, which serves as verified identification within the system. This structured process benefits farmers by organizing their records digitally, reducing manual documentation, improving credibility, and providing official verification that can support traceability and potential market opportunities.
In addition to the admin side, the process begins with secure login and access to submitted farmer records. The admin reviews each submission thoroughly, ensuring that all required personal, farm, affiliation, and production details are complete and valid. The review process directly includes approval or rejection decisions. If approved, the system activates the farmer’s account, granting verified status and QR code access. If rejected, the admin notifies the farmer to update specific information, ensuring data accuracy before activation. The admin can also view GI status and update farmer records when necessary, maintaining an up-to-date and reliable database. Overall, the system promotes data integrity, accountability, and transparency by requiring validation before activation. It benefits administrators by centralizing farmer information into a manageable digital database, while ensuring that only verified and qualified farmers are officially recognized within the platform.

Conceptual Data Flow Diagram



Figure 5. Conceptual DFD of Beanthentic System

This figure presents a high-level overview of the interaction between the Farmer, the Beanthentic System, and the Admin, highlighting the flow of registration, validation, and feedback within the platform. The process begins when the farmer submits profiling data through a registration form, which includes essential information such as personal details, farm profile, affiliations, and production records. The Beanthentic System then stores the submitted data in the database and forwards the registration details to the admin for review and approval.
On the admin side, the administrator evaluates the submitted information and decides whether to approve or reject the registration. The decision is sent back to the system, which then communicates the result to the farmer through a single response that includes registration confirmation, generated QR code, and notification of registration status. This process ensures efficient data management, proper validation, and clear communication between the farmer and the admin while maintaining a secure and organized system.

Low Level Data Flow Diagram




Figure 6. Low Level DFD of Beanthentic System

The diagram illustrates how data flows through the system, beginning with the farmer as the primary source of information. The process starts when the farmer submits account details through P1 (Register Farmer Account), which are forwarded to the admin for approval and then stored in the Beanthentic Central Database (D1). At the same time, the farmer provides farm profiling data through P2 (Encode Farm Profile Data). This profiling data is saved in the database and later retrieved by P3 (Data Preparation), where raw profiling inputs are cleaned and converted into a structured dataset. This structured data is then sent back to the central database, making it available for further processing and analysis.
Once the data is prepared, P4 (Random Forest GI Eligibility Analysis) accesses the structured dataset from the database to evaluate the farmer’s eligibility for Geographic Indication (GI). The evaluation results are sent to the admin for review and verification, ensuring that decisions are validated before proceeding. After the farmer is approved and verified, P5 (Generate QR Code for Digital Farmer Profile) retrieves the complete farmer record from the database and generates a unique QR code for identification. In addition, the system supports communication and transaction handling through the messaging module and transaction processing components, which exchange messages, store records, and generate receipts between the farmer and admin. Overall, the Beanthentic Central Database serves as the central hub that connects all processes, enabling efficient data storage, validation, analysis, and output generation.













Entity Relationship Diagram



Figure 7.  ERD of Beanthentic System

Figure 7 presents the major entities, their attributes, and the relationships within the Beanthentic system as illustrated in the diagram. The central entity is Farmer, which serves as the core of the system and is linked to both Personal Information and Farm Information. The Personal Information entity stores details such as first name, last name, barangay, and RSBSA registration data, while Farm Information captures agricultural data including total plant area, ownership status, and the number of bearing and non-bearing coffee trees categorized into varieties such as robusta, liberica, and excelsa. The Farmer entity is also associated with the Production entity, which records the quantity of harvested coffee per variety and tracks remaining beans, providing a clear view of each farmer’s production output.
In addition, the system includes operational and support entities that facilitate transactions and communication. The Transaction entity records sales data such as product, quantity, amount, payment method, and transaction date, all linked to a specific farmer. Communication within the system is handled through Message and Notification entities, enabling user interaction and system alerts. Administrative control is managed through the Admin and Activity Log entities, which track user activities and system changes. Furthermore, the Updates entity allows posting of announcements or content with titles, images, and engagement metrics, while the Maps entity stores location-related data and coffee variety distribution per farmer. The IPOPHIL entity is also included to manage intellectual property-related records of farmers. Overall, the diagram reflects an integrated system that supports farmer profiling, farm management, production monitoring, transactions, and administrative functions






Database Schema


Figure 8.  Data Schema of Beanthentic System


	This figure illustrates the structured tables, their primary keys (PK), foreign keys (FK), and relationships of the Beanthentic system. Three related tables make up the geographical hierarchy: Province (ProvinceID, Province_Name), which is connected to Municipality via ProvinceID, and Municipality, which is further connected to Barangay to form the entire location structure. The Farmer table, which has FarmerID (PK), BarangayID (FK), FAOfficerID (FK), Farmer_Name, Birthday, and RSBARegistered, is at the core of the structure. This table connects each farmer to a designated agricultural officer listed in the FA_Officer database (FAOfficerID, Officer_Name) as well as to a particular barangay.
	The FarmerOwnership table, which links FarmerID and OwnershipTypeID to the OwnershipType table that describes several ownership categories, is used to manage farm ownership information. InventoryID (PK), FarmerID (FK), StatusID (FK), VarietyID (FK), and NumberOfTrees are among the tree inventory information kept in the FarmerTreeInventory table, which is linked to the TreeStatus and CoffeeVariety tables to categorize tree condition and variety. The ProductionRecord table, which links production statistics to both farmers and certain coffee types, provides ProductionID (PK), FarmerID (FK), VarietyID (FK), Year, TotalProductionKilos, NCPRS, and Remarks.


Development & Implementation Plan 
The development of Beanthentic followed the Agile Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) Model, enabling iterative development, continuous refinement, and regular validation through structured phases such as requirements analysis, design, development, testing, deployment, and maintenance. 
Deployment & Testing Plan (Infrastructure/Deployment)
Project Schedule 








Figure 9.  Development Plan of Beanthentic System

   Planning (January 06 – February 28, 2026)
	The planning phase began on January 6 and concluded on February 28, 2026. During this period, the foundation of Beanthentic was established through literature review, problem identification, and consultations with coffee farmers. An adviser orientation ensured alignment with academic standards. The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) was completed, detailing functional and non-functional requirements, system objectives, QR code traceability framework, and the initial product backlog.
   Design (March 1 – March 11, 2026)
	The design phase focused on developing the system architecture, database schema, and UI/UX wireframes for both web and mobile platforms. Data Flow Diagrams (DFDs) mapped the movement of data from farmer registration to QR-enabled traceability. The design was finalized and validated before development began.
   Development – Core Functionalities (March 13 – May)
Core features were developed, including farmer profiling, data management, QR code generation, and the analytics dashboard. These features formed the primary operational components of the system.
   Development – Non-Functional Requirements (April 3 – May)
This phase focused on enhancing system performance, usability, security, responsiveness, and interface improvements to ensure efficiency and user satisfaction.
   Testing (June - July)

System testing was conducted from June to August 2026. This included unit testing, integration testing, system testing, and User Acceptance Testing (UAT) to ensure reliability, functionality, and usability.
   Deployment (July – August)

Deployment activities began in June and continued until August 2026. The system was prepared for implementation, configured for actual use, and finalized for operational readiness.
   Monitoring (September - January 2027)

Post-deployment monitoring was conducted in August 2026 to evaluate system performance, address potential issues, and ensure stability after implementation.

Ethical Considerations
This study strictly adhered to established ethical standards in the development and evaluation of the Beanthentic system involving coffee farmers in Lipa City, Batangas. Prior to participation, informed consent was obtained from all participants. The purpose of the study, the nature of the Random Forest–driven and QR code–based profiling system, and the procedures involved in data collection were clearly explained to ensure transparency and understanding. Participation was entirely voluntary, and participants were informed of their right to withdraw at any time without penalty or negative consequences.
Data collection was limited to structured profiling forms and system evaluation questionnaires grounded in the ISO/IEC 25010 and Technology Acceptance Model frameworks. No interviews, audio recordings, video recordings, or covert observations were conducted. All collected data were treated with strict confidentiality, and sensitive personal identifiers were protected within the system database. QR codes generated by the system were designed to support traceability while ensuring controlled and authorized access to farmer profile information.
The Random Forest–based GI eligibility profiling feature of Beanthentic functions solely as a decision-support and documentation-readiness tool and does not replace official certification authorities such as the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines. AI-generated outputs reflect compliance patterns based on submitted data and predefined parameters and are not official eligibility determinations. All data were used exclusively for academic and research purposes, and ethical clearance was secured prior to implementation to ensure that the study was conducted responsibly, truthfully, and with full respect for the rights and welfare of the participants.

GEOGRAPHICAL INDICATION APPLICATION
Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL)

MANUAL OF SPECIFICATIONS
for the Geographical Indication

KAPENG BARAKO
(Coffea liberica W.Bull)

Province of Batangas and Province of Cavite, CALABARZON, Philippines

Prepared by:
[Applicant Organization / Cooperative Name]
[Address], Batangas / Cavite, Philippines

Date of Preparation: ______________________



NOTICE ON DATA GAPS AND EVIDENCE REQUIREMENTS: Sections marked with [FIELD DATA NEEDED] require primary data from farmers, cooperatives, and government agencies not available at the time of drafting. Applicants must supplement this document with sworn statements, farm records, laboratory analyses, and certifications from the relevant LGUs and national agencies prior to final submission to IPOPHL.

SECTION 1: IDENTIFICATION OF THE PRODUCT AND APPLICANT


SECTION 2: DESCRIPTION OF THE GEOGRAPHICAL AREA

2.1 Delineated Production Zone
The geographical area for the Kapeng Barako GI encompasses the historically established and scientifically validated coffee-producing territories of the Province of Batangas and the Province of Cavite, both within the CALABARZON (Region IV-A) administrative region of the Philippines.

Batangas Province: Coffee farming is concentrated in the municipalities surrounding Taal Lake, including Lipa City, Taal, Lemery, Agoncillo, Calaca, Balayan, and adjoining barangays. The province is the historical heartland of Barako cultivation, with commercial production documented since the 18th century when Spanish friars first planted Coffea liberica in the region (Slow Food Foundation, 2018). Field validation of C. liberica farms has confirmed highly suitable areas in Quezon and Batangas provinces (Garcia et al., 2021).

Cavite Province: Historically significant Barako-producing areas include Tagaytay City, Gen. Mariano Alvarez, and adjoining municipalities. Cavite has been documented as a second core province for C. liberica cultivation, with molecular and morphological differentiation studies having been conducted on coffee varieties grown in its farms (Cao et al., 2014, as cited in Balan et al., 2026).


2.2 Geological and Volcanic Soil Character
A defining feature of the Batangas production zone is its proximity to Taal Volcano, one of the most active volcanoes in the Philippines. Volcanic activity has historically produced Andisols – soils derived from volcanic ash and tephra – which are among the most fertile agricultural soils in the world. Research on volcanic soils documents that Andisols are characterized by high porosity and drainage, elevated levels of phosphorus, potassium, boron, iron, and zinc, light and spongy texture enabling deep root penetration, and amorphous clay minerals such as allophane and imogolite that contribute to unique cation exchange capacity (Mihai et al., 2023). Coffee thrives on Andisols specifically because of this mineral richness and favorable drainage properties. The 2020 Taal Volcano eruption, while damaging to existing Barako farms – with thousands of trees affected in 2020 and 2021 (Aguilar et al., 2021) – is expected to further enrich and replenish the mineral composition of soils in the medium to long term, consistent with documented volcanic soil recovery dynamics (Mihai et al., 2023).

2.3 Agroforestry Landscape and Ecological Context
Barako farms in Lipa City, Batangas operate within a complex agroforestry landscape. Ecological network mapping in the Lipa area has documented coffee landscapes intercropped with fruit-bearing trees and perennial shade crops, which support predator-prey dynamics for natural pest control and contribute to the distinctive growing microclimate of Barako farms. This agroforestry structure – consistent with C. liberica’s natural origin as a rainforest-adapted species – influences the flavor development and morphological expression of the coffee. Similar agroforestry designs have been studied at cacao farms in Laguna and Batangas, where the interaction of AMF (arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi) with soil microbiota in intercropped systems has been shown to enhance soil nitrogen dynamics and organic matter levels (Paguntalan et al., 2023).

SECTION 3: DESCRIPTION OF THE PRODUCT

3.1 Botanical Identity and General Description
Kapeng Barako refers exclusively to coffee produced from Coffea liberica W.Bull (family Rubiaceae), the Liberica species of coffee. C. liberica is one of only four commercially cultivated coffee species globally and is among the rarest, accounting for approximately 1–2% of world coffee production (Aguilar et al., 2021; Balan et al., 2026). The Philippines holds a competitive advantage as one of only three countries – besides Ethiopia and Malaysia – recognized for producing Coffea liberica (Aguilar et al., 2021).

The name “Barako” derives from the Tagalog word for “wild boar,” referencing the animal’s fondness for the plant’s leaves and berries, and has evolved into a cultural shorthand for strength, boldness, and uncompromising quality (Slow Food Foundation, 2018). C. liberica was first planted in Batangas by Spanish friars in the 18th century, and by the 1800s, Philippines-grown Barako was being exported to the United States; at its peak in the 19th century, the Philippines was the fourth-largest coffee-producing country in the world (Slow Food Foundation, 2018).

3.2 Plant Morphological Characteristics
The following morphometric parameters are based on baseline data from Batangas C. liberica populations (Balan et al., 2026; Aguilar et al., 2021; Fernandez et al., 2022 as cited in Balan et al., 2026) and from comparative morphological studies referenced in the literature:


Note: The strong positive correlation between leaf area and cherry volume (r = 0.84, p = 0.001) and between leaf area and bean volume (r = 0.92, p < 0.001) documented by Balan et al. (2026) indicates coordinated morphological development. This means leaf morphology can serve as a practical field indicator of bean size potential – relevant for farm-level selection and quality monitoring.

Compared to other commercial coffee species, C. liberica is distinctive in producing the largest leaves (max length up to 224 mm vs. 208 mm for C. canephora and 137 mm for C. arabica) and the largest fruit (length x width: 1.8–3.4 cm x 1.7–3.3 cm, compared to smaller dimensions in arabica and robusta). The bean shape is asymmetrical – one side is lower than the other, creating a distinctive hook or point at the bottom, and the furrow in the middle is typically jagged rather than straight (Slow Food Foundation, 2018; Balan et al., 2026).

The trees themselves grow notably taller than other coffee species, reaching up to 20 meters, and are self-pollinating. They produce their fruit at lower elevations (400–1,200 m asl) than C. arabica (Garcia et al., 2021; Slow Food Foundation, 2018). Coffee plants demonstrate adaptability to different growing conditions, with high drought survival rates and optimal performance at altitudes of 600–1,000 m above sea level (Balan et al., 2026).

3.3 Sensory and Cup Quality Characteristics
Kapeng Barako from Batangas and Cavite is recognized for a distinctive sensory profile that differentiates it from other commercial coffee species:


FIELD DATA NEEDED: Official cupping scores (SCA protocol), specific flavor wheel descriptors from certified Q-Graders, and chemical composition data (caffeine content, chlorogenic acids) for Batangas/Cavite Barako must be obtained from accredited laboratories and included as annexes.

SECTION 4: LINK BETWEEN THE PRODUCT AND ITS GEOGRAPHICAL ORIGIN

4.1 Natural Factors
The unique quality and reputation of Kapeng Barako are attributable to the specific combination of natural and human factors present in the delineated geographical area:

4.1.1 Volcanic Soil Influence (Andisols)
The Batangas production zone lies in the direct volcanic influence zone of Taal Volcano, one of the most historically active volcanoes in the Philippines. Volcanic ash deposits create Andisols characterized by mineral richness (phosphorus, potassium, boron, iron, zinc), high organic matter capacity, excellent drainage, and light spongy texture. Coffee – specifically C. liberica – thrives in these soils because of the mineral availability and drainage properties (Mihai et al., 2023). The volcanic origin of the soil is directly linked to the bold and intense flavor profile of Kapeng Barako, which coffee experts have long attributed in part to the exceptional mineral-rich growing medium. AMF (arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi) associations common in the CALABARZON agroforest systems further mediate nitrogen and phosphorus uptake in ways that influence crop nutrition and development (Paguntalan et al., 2023).

4.1.2 Climate and Elevation
The provinces of Batangas and Cavite sit within the CALABARZON climate zone, characterized by a warm humid tropical climate with two pronounced seasons. The optimal elevation range of 300–600 m asl in the core production zones of Batangas (Lipa City area at approximately 328 m asl) corresponds precisely with the documented optimal growing range for C. liberica (400–600 m asl per Garcia et al., 2021). The combination of warm temperatures (21–26°C), adequate but not excessive rainfall (2,500–3,000 mm annually), and volcanic soils creates conditions that are difficult or impossible to replicate outside this specific geography. This is reflected in the land suitability analysis showing that Batangas and Cavite rank among the highest-suitable areas in the Philippines for C. liberica production, with Quezon and Batangas classified as highly suitable and Iloilo and Davao del Sur as only moderately suitable (Garcia et al., 2021).

4.1.3 Agroforestry Microclimate
The agroforestry landscape of Barako-producing areas in Lipa and surrounding municipalities creates a natural shading system. The shade from intercropped fruit trees and coconuts moderates temperature extremes and controls light exposure, which is documented to slow the ripening of coffee cherries – a process that contributes to the development of more complex flavor compounds. This ecological function is consistent with the documented relationship between leaf morphology and fruit development found in C. liberica populations from Batangas (Balan et al., 2026).

4.2 Human Factors
4.2.1 Historical and Cultural Heritage
Kapeng Barako has a documented history exceeding 250 years in Batangas. Spanish friars planted Coffea liberica in Batangas in the 18th century, and by the 19th century, the variety had become the economic backbone of the province, with the Philippines briefly reaching the status of the 4th largest coffee-producing nation globally. The name “Barako” – meaning wild boar in Tagalog – became synonymous with the powerful and untamed character of the coffee (Slow Food Foundation, 2018). This centuries-long cultivation has produced locally adapted planting material, farm management knowledge, and processing traditions that are specific to the Batangas and Cavite context.

Note on species-origin link: While Coffea liberica was first documented by William Hiern in 1876 and originates from West Africa, the variety now cultivated in Batangas and Cavite has been shaped by more than two centuries of selection, adaptation to Andisol volcanic soils, and traditional cultivation practices unique to this region. This local adaptation is reflected in the morphological variation documented between farms in different locations (Aguilar et al., 2021), supporting the argument that the current Batangas/Cavite C. liberica population constitutes a geographically distinct product.

4.2.2 Traditional Use Patterns
In Batangas, Kapeng Barako serves a culinary function beyond that of a simple beverage. It is traditionally used as an alternative to soup (sabaw) when eating local dried fish from Taal Lake (tapa, dried fish, or other dry/fried dishes). This unique culinary integration is absent in coffee-producing regions outside Batangas and represents a human dimension of the product’s character that is geographically anchored (Slow Food Foundation, 2018; 43 Factory Coffee, 2024).

4.2.3 Traditional Processing Methods
Barako from Batangas is traditionally processed using the wet/washed method, involving hand-picking of ripe cherries, gentle pounding with wooden pestles to extract beans, washing to remove mucilage, sun-drying on bamboo mats or fabric for 1–2 weeks, additional drying after shell removal, and pan-roasting over wood-fired stoves with careful temperature control to achieve deep brown color (43 Factory Coffee, 2024). These traditional methods, passed down through generations of Batangueño farmers, contribute directly to the characteristic bold, pungent aroma and intense flavor profile that defines Kapeng Barako.

SECTION 5: PRODUCTION METHODS AND STANDARDS

5.1 Cultivation Requirements

5.2 Harvesting Standards
Cherries must be hand-picked at full maturity (deep red color; no green or over-ripe cherries in GI-certified lots)
Selective picking only; strip picking is not permitted for GI-labeled product
Peak harvest season: typically October–February (dry season) for primary crop
[FIELD DATA NEEDED: Local harvest calendar confirmed by participating farmers]

5.3 Post-Harvest Processing
5.3.1 Washed/Wet Process (Traditional Method – Primary)
Cherry sorting: Remove defective, damaged, or under-ripe cherries
Pulping: Hand-pulping using traditional wooden pestle, or mechanical pulper
Fermentation: Wet fermentation to remove mucilage (12–36 hours, or as traditionally practiced; water quality must be potable)
Washing: Thorough washing with clean water to remove all fermentation residue
Sun-drying: Spread beans on raised drying beds, bamboo mats, or fabric; 1–2 weeks until moisture ≤12%
Hulling: Remove parchment layer after drying
Grading and sorting: Remove defective beans

5.3.2 Natural/Dry Process (Permitted Alternative)
Whole cherry drying on raised beds is permitted as an alternative method. Processing parameters and quality results must be declared on labeling.

5.4 Roasting (for Roasted Coffee GI Products)
Roasting must be conducted within the delineated geographical area OR by licensed roasters who comply with GI standards
Traditional wood-fired pan-roasting is recognized as an authentic production method
Target: Medium to dark roast achieving deep brown color without excessive charring
Post-roast resting: Minimum 24 hours before packaging
[FIELD DATA NEEDED: Roast profiles (time, temperature curves) from established local roasters]

5.5 Quality Parameters

SECTION 6: LABELING AND PACKAGING REQUIREMENTS

6.1 Mandatory Label Elements
The GI name "KAPENG BARAKO" must appear prominently on all certified products
The designation "Geographical Indication" and IPOPHL registration number must be displayed
Province of origin (Batangas / Cavite) must be declared
Species declaration: Coffea liberica
Processing method (washed / natural) must be declared
Lot number and traceability code
Name and address of registered producer or roaster
Net weight and date of production/packaging

6.2 GI Seal Usage
The official IPOPHL GI seal may only be affixed to products that have undergone certification inspection by the authorized control body and meet all standards in this Manual of Specifications. Unauthorized use of the GI name or seal is subject to enforcement under RA 8293 (Intellectual Property Code of the Philippines) and IPOPHL MC No. 2022-022.

6.3 Packaging Standards
Green beans: Food-grade jute or GrainPro bags; labeled with producer, origin, harvest year, and lot number
Roasted beans: Food-grade packaging with one-way valve for degassing; best-before date within 12 months of roasting
Ground coffee: Food-grade packaging; best-before within 6 months of roasting

SECTION 7: CONTROL AND INSPECTION

7.1 Control Body
[FIELD DATA NEEDED]: The applicant must designate or establish an authorized control body, which may include the relevant Provincial Agriculture Offices of Batangas and Cavite, the Philippine Coffee Board, the Bureau of Agriculture and Fisheries Standards (BAFS), or a duly accredited third-party certification body.

7.2 Inspection Points

7.3 Record-Keeping Requirements
All registered producers must maintain farm logs (planting date, variety, inputs, harvest dates)
Processing records for each lot (processing method, dates, quantities)
Sales records with buyer information for traceability
Records must be made available to inspectors upon request and retained for minimum 5 years

SECTION 8: HISTORY, REPUTATION, AND TRADITIONAL KNOWLEDGE

8.1 Historical Record
The historical presence of Coffea liberica in Batangas is among the most well-documented agricultural histories in the Philippines:


8.2 Recognition and Awards
Included in the Slow Food Ark of Taste (Slow Food Foundation, 2018): International recognition of Kapeng Barako as an endangered traditional food product with unique sensory and cultural heritage value
Philippine Coffee Industry Roadmap (2017–2022): Government recognition of Liberica as a target species for increased production to reduce import dependency
Growing interest in the international specialty coffee market, with premium Barako lots achieving premium pricing (Balan et al., 2026; Davis et al., 2022 as cited in Balan et al., 2026)
